Of course, these tools’ successful adoption and efficacy would be influenced by

the industry’s willingness to embrace ethical design standards and integrate such

support. However, this integration is a necessary embodiment of ethical princi-
ples rather than a strategy to enhance tool efficacy. It requires a broader shift

towards embedding these standards deeply within development cultures. Besides,

developing such software products demands an insightful grasp of player psychol-
ogy founded on research surrounding cognitive bias and DPs and the pragmatics

of game development. Rigorous empirical testing will also be essential to guar-
antee that such tools are effective and easy to use, balance the empowerment of

both end-users and developers’ sustainable goals, and foster a healthy interactive

experience.

It is important to note that while designing developer-support tools is cru-
cial for fostering ethical game design practices, it is equally essential to recognize

the structural constraints within the game industry that may limit their adop-
tion and impact. Many monetization-related decisions are typically made not

by designers or developers but by higher-level stakeholders such as sharehold-
ers, executives, and product or monetization teams. These decision-makers often

have limited or no background in game development and primarily rely on key

performance indicators (KPIs) like player retention, session length, active user

base, and revenue metrics to drive design directives. As a result, developers and

designers may have little autonomy to reject manipulative practices, even when

they are aware of the ethical concerns surrounding DPs. Given this context, we

advocate for further empirical research – such as large-scale surveys or interviews

with industry professionals, especially within the mobile and live-ops sectors –

to better understand developers’ awareness of DPs, their perceived agency in

decision-making processes, and the organizational pressures they face. This line

of inquiry could help clarify how deeply knowledge and decision power regarding

DPs are distributed across different roles in game companies, potentially guiding

more targeted and feasible counter-strategies in the future.

3.3 Advancing Methods and Measures for Assessing Dark Pattern

Prevalence and Player Experience, Including Well-Being

Current HCI research excels at identifying and categorizing DPs, although not

as much within games, and provides critical explorations of their ethical and

psychological impacts [ 16 ]. Significant steps have been made toward evaluation

tools, such as the System Darkness Scale [ 30 ] that assess a system’s perceived

“darkness,” and frameworks like the ADD framework [ 8 ] for critically considering

DPs in children’s applications. While these analytical insights and identification

methods are foundational, we advocate for expanding efforts to develop and val-
idate robust methods and measures that can more directly and quantifiably

assess the impact of specific game design elements on player autonomy,

perceived manipulation, and holistic psychological well-being.

The aim is not merely to identify whether well-being is affected but to under-
stand and quantify this relationship with greater nuance, particularly when

evaluating the efficacy of proposed countermeasures. It involves developing or

From Understanding to Intervention 97

adapting specific player experience instruments, such as validated questionnaires

or carefully designed behavioral metrics, that explicitly capture core tenets of

ethical interaction. These instruments should focus on perceived autonomy, fair-
ness, transparency, the sense of being respected (or manipulated), and critical

aspects of psychological well-being, drawing inspiration from well-established

theories like the Self-Determination Theory [ 33 , 34 ]. Such measures would allow

researchers to move beyond general assessments of “darkness” to indicate how

specific patterns or their alternatives influence these fundamental human needs,

a necessary point of departure to investigate how to counteract them.

Building upon existing frameworks, we call for creating standardized yet

adaptable methodologies for evaluating both the presence and, crucially, the

impact of DPs across diverse game genres and monetization models. It includes

refining our approaches to measure the actual effect of interventions designed

to mitigate DPs or enhance player awareness. For example, understanding why

some educational interventions show limited impact on knowledge about DPs

matters [ 39 ] requires more sensitive evaluation protocols to determine true effi-
cacy and identify areas for improvement.

Addressing these challenges involves not only identifying the absence

of DPs but also evaluating the effectiveness of ethical design choices

in creating a positive, engaging game experience driven by genuine enjoyment,

not coercion. We can enhance our use of gameplay data by developing teleme-
try and behavioral analytics to uncover patterns that indicate compromised

player autonomy or manipulative mechanics. Integrating this data with qual-
itative insights and refined player experience tools can lead to a more compre-
hensive assessment. Additionally, we could improve methodologies for assessing

the prevalence of DPs in new games by combining expert evaluations tailored to

specific game types and monetization strategies, along with emerging automated

detection approaches where ethically appropriate.

Developing and adapting methods and validated measures is not an end in

itself. Instead, it is a step toward generating highly specific, empirically grounded

guidelines that practitioners can trust and readily apply. These methods will

allow us to move from general advice to concrete, evidence-backed recommen-
dations (e.g., “ To uphold player autonomy in reward systems, design X which
demonstrably leads to Y outcome in perceived fairness, as measured by Z ”). By

focusing on quantifiable impacts on core aspects of ethical player experience,

we can make assessments more systematic, comparable across studies, and ulti-
mately more impactful in driving real change in game design practices.

This position paper argued for systematically expanding the focus of HCI games

Defining Hierarchical Scaling and Contextual Variants for RPs Discus-
sion revealed that original RPs failed to account for genre-specific constraints,
platform limitations, or player profiles. Contextual differences, such as the transi-
tion from single-player to multiplayer, are not isolated exceptions but structural
adaptations required to maintain the pattern’s efficacy. By analyzing these re-
quirements, we established two pragmatic rules for framework expansion:
1. Progressive Requirement Scaling : Structure pattern application into
hierarchical tiers, each representing increasing psychological need satisfaction
from a baseline of non-frustration.
2. Environment-Based Subclassing : Define structural variants that adapt
universal levels to specific gameplay contexts (e.g., genre, mode, platform)
without changing core logic.
These rules allow a more precise integration across varied RP titles. For
instance, the core mechanic of Companion requires different implementations
for decorative mascots in The Sims compared to combat partners in World of
Warcraft . Similarly, Creative Suite spans a broad design space—from aesthetic
customization to complex scenario sharing—that cannot be addressed by a single
description without losing developer utility.

Following progressive scaling, patterns are organized into universal applica-
tion levels. Level L1 establishes the ethical floor of non-frustration. While L1
represents standard practice, i.e., its inclusion in the framework identifies it as a
necessary boundary against deceptive monetization or retention tactics, L2 and
L3 progressively enhance need satisfaction. For example, Open Gate includes
L1 – Safety (automatic progress saving), L2 – Autonomy (intentional stopping),
and L3 – Competence (visual feedback reinforcing achievement).
The use of environment-based subclassing through variants ensures extensi-
bility. This dual structure allows practitioners to add contextual implementations
to the RP catalog while preserving each pattern’s conceptual identity.

An Updated Radiant Pattern Framework Workshop evaluations and re-
finement sessions confirmed that original pattern descriptions lacked the struc-
tural rigor required for industry application. The primary failure involved the
conflation of developer goals with player outcomes, which obscured how specific
design choices support ethical objectives. Furthermore, the absence of explicit
dimensions like genre or platform prevented the framework from capturing the
structural adaptations necessary for diverse play environments. Table 3 presents
the resulting template. This systematic structure reorganizes the Radiant Pat-
tern Framework, ensuring that every RP added to the catalog supports consistent
application and future extensibility without fragmenting conceptual integrity.
To ensure scalability of the RP framework, we defined four pragmatic rules
for the RP template:
1. Goal–Outcome Decoupling : Separate developers’ technical goals from

Player Problems (the experiential goals or need frustrations addressed).
2. Multi-Dimensional Scoping : Specify target actors and context to avoid
vague terminology and support diverse settings.
3. Invariant–Variant Duality : Define core properties (Invariants) that must
hold across adaptations to preserve identity, regardless of the Variant.
4. Traceable Need Satisfaction : Map each solution to hierarchical design
levels (L1–L3) to validate radiance through structural criteria.

5 A Catalog of Games Radiant Patterns

The Radiant Patterns Catalog 
6 
is a structured knowledge system designed to
bridge player well-being research and game development practice. It operational-
izes the multidimensional framework of Universal Levels and Contextual Vari-
ants derived from our refinement sessions. The platform is organized around
context-driven filters that allow practitioners and researchers to query patterns
according to developer goals and player needs, directly reflecting Phase I findings
on genre specificity and application context. The system distinguishes between
Finalized RPs – those validated through formal verification – and Candidate
RPs, which are undergoing co-creation. This separation enables transparency re-
garding pattern maturity while allowing users to choose between peer-validated
standards and experimental alternatives. Filters include variant-based con-
texts (e.g., Single-Player, Multiplayer) and development goals (e.g., preserving
progress, managing companions), all within the boundaries of the RP framework.
A core contribution of the platform is its tiered visualization of pattern levels,
translating abstract psychological principles into concrete design examples. Each
pattern presents its Universal Application Levels (L1, L2, L3) alongside a visual
carousel of real-world game instances. These examples, combined with textual
explanations, function as a semiotic bridge that illustrates how an RP manifests
across levels without requiring deep SDT expertise.
To ensure scalability, the platform includes a collaboration module en-
abling repository expansion. It supports two entry types: structured submissions ,
where contributors propose new patterns or variants using the RP template
vocabulary; and problem-based contributions , which document recurring design
problems requiring ethical alternatives. All submissions are flagged as Candi-
dates and remain visible but distinct from validated RPs until reviewed through
the governance process, preserving transparency while maintaining reliability.
To safeguard integrity, we propose a governance model in which community-
proposed RPs undergo a formal verification protocol modeled after the collabo-
rative workshops described in this paper. Sessions involving both academic and
industry specialists assess submissions against defined RP Invariants. Rather
than binary acceptance, proposals return to contributors for iterative refine-
ment, ensuring that candidate patterns remain accessible while being polished
into finalized standards. We invite volunteers from academia and industry to
participate as reviewers. Although reliance on a self-selected community may
introduce selection bias or uneven SDT expertise, the documentation template
serves as the primary objective check. By requiring mechanics to be mapped to
specific needs, it reduces the risk of subjective gatekeeping.

The autoethnography identified RPs in released games, confirming their real-

as DPs were identified through critical observation of manipulative practices in
the game industry[56], analyzing game structures through the RPs framework
allowed researchers to identify design practices that either avoid needs frustration
or support the fulfillment of basic psychological needs. The structural evolution
of the RP framework from generalized formulations to context-specific variants
addresses a core challenge in player experience research which is the inability to
account for unique, genre-specific interactions [28].
By establishing universal levels alongside these variants, the Radiant Pat-
terns framework a contextually-specific approach, recognizing that the ethical
impact of a mechanic is grounded in the unique characteristics of its gameplay
environment[3]. It is important to clarify that the Universal Levels (L1-L3) are
intended as a methodological baseline rather than a claim of universal experi-
ence. While the experiential reality of a patterns varies wildly between genres,
such as the difference between competence in a sandbox and a soulslike, the re-
quirement to not frustrate basic psychological needs remains the common ethical
denominator. Hence, the RP variants allow the lexicon to remain stable while
respecting these diverse contextual boundaries identified in the literature.
The common lexicon aims to offer a systematic alternative to rapid-response
research triggered by technology panics [41]. Yet, a shared vocabulary is a tool
for interaction design, not a solution for all ethical challenges. Systemic issues
such as game worker welfare, harassment, and online toxicity require regulatory
and cultural interventions that lie beyond the scope of interaction design [27].
Besides, identifying these new mechanics through autoethnography does not
automatically qualify them as Radiant Patterns. This is why they are referred
on findings as candidate RPs. Identifying an RP requires evidence of recurrence,
which establishes it as a pattern[2], as well as discussion and coherence with the
components defined by the framework. This distinction creates a logical need for
the Radiant Patterns Catalog (Section 5). Because a single autoethnographic
instance cannot confirm a pattern, and a 10-hour sample may not capture the
full systemic depth of complex titles, the Catalog serves as a filter where these
initial observations are flagged for further verification. The ’candidate’ ideas
are subjected to a verification protocol. This ensures that only those designs
proven to be recurring and ethically sound are finalized, transforming subjective
observations into community-validated design knowledge. Expert observation
may result in false positives, reinforcing the need for the Catalog’s collaborative
verification protocol in which the practical application of these patterns can be
observed, analyzed, and discussed collectively.
Current constraints include the absence of longitudinal testing. Establishing
the RP framework and catalog provides the technical foundation needed to move
toward support for positive impact. Yet, the RPs Catalog is the digital infrastruc-

observations into systematized, positive solutions. It offers the technical basis
for researchers and developers to co-create a repository of well-being-supportive
design patterns. This reinforces the development of a community centered on
ethical game design practices, fostering knowledge sharing and the adoption of

7 Final Remarks

This work evolves the RP framework by shifting focus to the structural non-
frustration of basic psychological needs through a refined lexicon, tiered levels,
and standardized templates. These components establish a system to connect
ethical research with game development practice. While this version lacks longi-
tudinal data, relies on a small expert-centric sample, and excludes systemic issues
like worker welfare or online toxicity, it establishes the technical foundation for
future industry-led verification.
Future work focuses on testing long-term impact, expanding the relatedness
dimension based on observed dialogue-driven instances, and implementing the
collaborative verification protocol to transition candidate patterns into finalized
standards. By providing this structure, the framework offers a technical path
for the industry to move beyond identifying dark patterns toward the active
co-creation of design cultures centered on player well-being

Abstract. Research on Dark or Deceptive Patterns (DPs) primarily fo-
cuses on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic)
contexts, leaving the understanding of DPs in the Global South largely
unexamined. This study analyzes DPs in 100 trending Android appli-
cations (apps) in Brazil. The results showed that 96% of the apps have
at least one DP, averaging 7.51 DPs per app, and 46% of them con-
tain at least 7 DPs. We identified six previously unreported DP cases in
the Brazilian context, demonstrating novel applications of known DPs.
We compared our results with previous studies conducted in Japanese
and American contexts, examining common subclasses and approaches
to addressing the identified differences in culture, wealth, and education.

1 Introduction

Dark Patterns (DPs) are user interface design choices that lead users to make
decisions they might not have made otherwise, often for the benefit of an online
service [9]. DPs often result in user behaviors that are against their best interests,
such as impulsive buying and installing applications (apps) that they do not
need [2]. The nature and impacts of DPs have been drawing attention from the
Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) community [7]. Although numerous studies
on DPs have focused on categorizing [13,8] and identifying the impacts [18,14]
of these patterns, those occurred primarily within Western and Anglocentric
societies [17], so it is crucial to understand how different countries recognize
and experience DPs in their interactions with digital interfaces.
For instance, when replicating Di Geronimo’s procedure, Hidaka et al. [20]
discovered a new class of DP called "Linguistic Dead Ends", which discourages
or prevents users from understanding the interface and/or content of an app

2 L. Ribeiro et al.

by manipulating language at a fundamental level. Hidaka’s findings reveal that
DPs were less prevalent in the Japanese context, with an average of 3.9 compared
to 7.4 found on Di Geronimo’s report. Consequently, our understanding of DP
prevalence and manifestation, often based on taxonomies developed in these
contexts, may not fully capture the situation in the Global South. As such, the
topics studied in DPs may differ in non-WEIRD countries.
Further, determining whether the Brazilian context is WEIRD or non-WEIRD
is difficult, due to its complex social indicators [11]. The complexity of this sit-
uation creates new challenges for the HCI community. Thus, it presents a criti-
cal context for investigation of DPs impact, representing a large digital market
within the Global South with specific characteristics in questions such as inequal-
ity in education [5], lack of digital literacy [21] and uneven spread of Information
and Communication Technologies (ICTs) [10], because of that we hypothesize
that DPs in Brazilian context have particularities.
Inspired by the culture-specific DPs found in Japan, which are linked to lin-
guistic characteristics [20], this work explores context-specific aspects in Brazil
regarding DPs. We aim to present baseline data on the Brazilian prevalence
and types of DPs, establishing a point of comparison with results from research
studies in the United States [3] and Japan [20]. Specifically, we investigate (i)
the frequency and types of DPs in the most widely used Brazilian apps, catego-
rized according to established classifications; (ii) how they contrast with previous
research conducted in other geographical settings.
To this end, we adapted the qualitative expert classification protocol of Di
Geronimo et al. [3] and included the DP class introduced by Hidaka et al. [20].
We analyzed the top 100 trending

2.1 Adaptations from the Original Protocol to Our Context

With the following adaptations, our work provides an initial classification of DPs

Recording and Classification. We added a test phase to determine our
recording method and find necessary protocol changes. For this, recording and

by Windows. Each researcher created a new Gmail account. We also purchased
a SIM card and plugged it into a smartphone to validate its use in apps that
required a phone number. To ensure consistency in the usage, we recorded the
first 10 minutes of the selected apps following eight tasks (when available): (i)
creating an account and log out; (ii) closing and reopening the app; (iii) visiting
the market page; (iv) going to the setting page; (v) checking the terms of service
and privacy policy; (vi) continuing shopping until checkout; (vii) trying to select
product names in e-shopping; (viii) using the app for its intended use. We did
not purchase any products or services in the apps.

2.3 DPs Classification

We organized ourselves into two pairs. While one pair was recording the usage,
the other was analyzing the videos. Once we had already analyzed the first
half of the apps, we switched roles. During the classification process, we first
analyzed the videos individually. Then, we discussed them together to mitigate
DP Blindness. The agreement between the pairs was good according to Weighted
Cohen’s Kappa ( κ = 0.64) which indicates substantial agreement. We included
a third researcher to break ties when the pair did not reach an agreement.
Di Geronimo’s expansion [3] of Gray’s taxonomy [9], together with Hidaka’s
later findings related to linguistic DPs [20], based our classification process.
Therefore, the taxonomy used in this study divides the DPs into six macro
classes: (i) Nagging; (ii) Obstruction including three subclasses (Intermediate
Currency, Price Comparison Prevention, and Roach Motel); (iii) Sneaking in-
cluding four subclasses (Bait and Switch, Hidden Information, Preselection, and
Sneak into Basket); (iv) Interface Interferences including five subclasses (Dis-
guised Ad, Aesthetic Manipulation, Toying with Emotions, False Hierarchy, and
Trick Question); (v) Forced Action including two subclasses (Privacy Zuchering
and Disguised Ad); (vi) Linguistic Dead-End including the subclass Untransla-
tion. Besides the macro class Linguistic Dead-Ends defined by Hidaka [20], the
macro classes and subclasses are defined in detail in Gray’s study [9].
Alongside the types of DPs, we also followed a guide of 40 specific DP
cases [16] to address the subjectivity of identifying DPs based solely on their
descriptions. There were DP cases that fit more directly with the macro class it-
self. For this reason, Nagging, Obstruction, and Forced Action are macro classes
that also function as unique subclasses within themselves. Additionally, to en-

3 Results

Among the 100 studied apps, 96% of them contained at least one DP, and pre-
sented a total of 751 DPs across all corpus, with an average of 7.51 DPs per
app (std.dev.:4,7), very similar to what was found by Di Geronimo [3] (avg.: 7.4,
std.dev: 5). Additionally, 13% (N=13) of the apps contained between 0 and 2
DPs, 41% (N=41) contained between 3 and 6 DPs, and 46% (N=46) of them
contained at least 7 DPs.
Between the six macro classes, apps contained an average of 3.7 macro classes
per app (std.dev.: 1.5). The most frequent was Nagging DPs appearing in 78%
(N=78) of the apps, followed by Interface Interference with 76% (N=76) and
Forced Action with 62% (N=62), as shown in Fig. 1.

Our findings also revealed six DP cases previously unreported in international
research. They demonstrate novel applications of known DPs: (i) “ Terms/Policy
in Another Language ” (Untranslation case) when crucial information for the
user (terms of service or privacy policy) is in another language, even if the app
is in the native user language, creating a barrier between the user and the in-
formation; (ii) “ Terms/Policy Out of Bounds ” (Obstruction case) redirects
the user to an external page, typically a web page, to access the terms of service
or privacy policy, increasing unnecessary stress and reducing the likelihood of
reading; (iii) “ Ads with layers ” (Obstruction case) specifies chains of multiple
time-delayed sub-ads to extend user exposure within the same content, making
more than one “attention call” in the same time span; (iv) “ Task-based Re-
wards ” (Forced Action case) describes cases where the app presents a mission
beyond the main flow, that when completed rewards the user with some aspect
of the app services; (v) “ Ad-locked Rewards ” (Forced Action case) indicates
when the user is forced to watch an advertisement to receive a reward like vir-
tual coins, time accelerators, or other bonuses; (vi) “ Evoke Emotions to Take
Action ” (Toying with Emotions case) specifies uses of any language or other
appealing visual elements to persuade the user into an action. Those DP cases

4 Discussions

The discovery of six new cases of dark patterns, which constitute approximately
21% of the reported DPs, provides a more specific and consistent classification
of these patterns. This new classification aligns the previous list of DP cases
more closely with the Brazilian context. Additionally, it suggests that apps in
Brazil (whether local or international) are employing innovative strategies to
discourage usage and prompt users to take action, beyond merely displaying ads
or pop-ups. These strategies often involve creating new tasks that engage users
in activities beneficial to the developer, such as enabling notifications for app
updates or using persuasive messages to encourage users to rate the app.
Our results indicate that the presence of DPs in Brazilian apps aligns closely
with those in American apps, with an average score of 7.51 compared to Di
Geronimo’s 7.4, and a prevalence of 96% versus Di Geronimo’s 95%. However,
the distribution of these results in the DP subclasses differentiates these two
scenarios. When analyzing the most recurring subclasses, it is interesting to
note that even though Nagging is in first place in both surveys, Brazilian apps
stand out in the percentage difference (34,5%).
A broader perspective on this distribution difference reveals that in Brazil,
apps often use DPs that aim to manipulate users by directing them to alternative
activities, while in the US, they tend to manipulate users by tricking them into
making specific decisions and taking certain actions. The three most common
DPs tried to obstruct or force the user to interact with the application. Therefore,
there is an increase in the number of cases involving Nagging and Forced Action
in the Brazilian context. Moreover, the fourth most common is Untranslation
(Linguistic Dead-Ends), appearing at least once in 45% of the apps.
However, when comparing our results with Hidaka’s findings [20], we found
an increase in presence per app on 10 out of the 16 subclasses considered in the
analyses. This suggests that the Japanese DP situation appears to be handled
more strictly compared to the Brazilian one. This could be due to cultural, le-
gal, and market differences. Further, the subclasses with the most increase were
Aesthetic Manipulation (171,40%), Unstranslation (100%) and Trick Question
(100%). The most decrease being Hidden Information (-116,60%), Roach Motal
(-100%), and Intermediate Currency (-60%). Furthermore, the substantial in-
crease in the Unstranslation subclass in the Brazilian context draws attention
to a misuse of language that intentionally obscures information by utilizing a
foreign language, even when the rest of the app is in the user’s native language.
Those differences, particularly the Untranslation, should be addressed in future
works about DPs in Brazil, since the population has a score considered low in
proficiency tests such as the EF English Proficiency Index [4].

The comparison of our findings with those of Di Geronimo and Hidaka reveals
differences in the expression of DPs in each context (e.g., the DP occurrence sur-
plus in 10 out of 16 subclasses, compared with Hidaka’s findings). This suggests
that various socioeconomic, educational, and sociocultural factors may influence
how, where, and when DPs are manifested. Future research conducted in vari-
ous contexts should expand this discussion and provide new insights into how
cultural differences influence the presence of DPs.

5 Limitations

Our scope contains trending free apps on the Brazilian Google Play Store. We
recorded 10 minutes of the first use of each app; any deviation from this prede-
termined scope may generate new and different results. Moreover, some interac-
tions—and consequently DPs—might be limited or vary in an extended usage
scenario. Despite the sample reduction, we found similar results, indicating that
the impact was not substantial.
The intention behind using the emulator was to replicate the experience of a
real smartphone. However, a specific subset of DPs may not appear in emulated
applications. In certain instances, specific apps were inaccessible because they
flagged the emulator as suspicious for usage.

6 Conclusion

After analyzing 100 trending mobile apps in Brazil, we found an average of 7.51
DPs/app and six new cases of use of known dark patterns in the Brazilian con-
text. The results showed key differences compared to contexts in the United
States [3] and Japan [20] (e.g., average DPs per app, common DP subclass).
Our findings enhance the understanding of DPs and their consequences in soci-
eties beyond the WEIRD classification, promoting a more comprehensive view
of the topic, especially within Brazilian culture. Future work should explore the
presence of DPs in Finance apps and expand research by using a larger corpus
that considers more representatives of the Global South and their unique as-
pects as non-WEIRD societies. We encourage the HCI community to broaden
its perspective and actively research how DPs affect society’s economy, popula-
tion well-being, and culture beyond the WEIRD spectrum.
